REPORT TO THE BOYS' CAMPING COM\ITTEE, 
MONTREAL YMCA. 


Gentlemen: 


It is unfortunate that the enrollment was down at Perrot this 
summer, for in every other way it was a most successful season. Even 
the weather was kind to us, during the daytime we had perfect camping 
westher, and although it rained at night, we had only one morning 
during the six weeks of boys' camp when it was necessary to have an 
indoor program. 


STAFF: 

Of the twenty-four staff members, only seven were new to Perrot, 
three senior staff, and four counsellors. All proved to be excellent 
camp people, with fine qualities too numerous to mention at this time. 
However, I would like to mention that Mrs. Iris Sirkin was the most 
efficient nurse we heave ever had. Archie Church, Junior Section 
Director, set a pace that kept everyone on their toes all summer, and 
Elwood Fletcher, with past experience at Camp Weredale, handled the 
Crafts program expertly. 


STAFF TRAINING: 

Staff training started with most of the counsellors attend- 
ing the "in-city" training sessions. This was followed by five days 
"in-camp" training. However, about half of this time was needed for 
work projects. 


VISITING DAYS: 
Opening camp on a Saturday, and limiting the visiting to 
one Sunday every two weeks, proved to be a very good plan. There was 
no homesickness to speak of, and only one camper went home on a visiting 
day. 


TENT UNIT, SECTION & sLL CAMP PROGRAM: 


Due to the low enrollment, each tent unit consisted of five 
or six campers, compared to the usual seven. This greatly facilitated 
all phases of the program. 


The counsellor was the leader for his own tent group for 
all activities, and was with his campers at all times. This demanded 
more skills of the counsellor, but gave more variety to his work and, 
most important, it gave better coverage. 


The tent unit planned its’ own program for part of most 
days. This was done through the Little Chiefs, the tent representatives, 
who met daily with the Section Director. 


Evening programs were usually. on a section basis, and 
consisted mainly of environmental games. 


-oO- 


The whole camp Yet for weekly Council Fires, Friendship 
Fires and General Swims. 


Thus there was a reasonably good balance among the three 
types of program. 


TRIPPING: 

Canoe trips were limited mainly to the Rangers, our oldest 
campers. Two five-day trips went to Carillon under the leadership 
of Mr. Tom MacFarlane, who volunteered his services for this job. 


His kindness saved our tripping program as we did not have adult 
leadership that could be spared for long canoe trips. There were several 
counsellor-led overnight trips to Windmill Foint, four miles from camp, 
and Pine Island, six miles from camp. 


All campers must reach the Swim Standards before they are allowed 
to go on canoe trips, and all campers wear life jackets while on the 
water at any time. 


HIKING: 

Mr. Rousseau, who owns part of Windmill Point, kindly gave us 
permission to use the picnic area for overnight hikes. It is a 
beautiful spot, and needless to say, we made the most of it. Every 
camper went on at least one hike during his stay at Perrot. 


COUNCIL FIRES: 

The weekly Council Fires were as popular as ever. The new 
Big Chiefs enjoyed the meetings as much as the campers. Many youngsters 
were given an opportunity to stand on the Council Rock and give their 
reports to the whole gathering. Many others took part in Pow-Wow Dances, 
Challenges and Pageants. It is truly amazing how receptive and sincere 
the campers are in this atmosphere. 


PENNY FAIR: 

Our Annual Penny Fair, along with a general campaign throughout 
the summer, netted $230.00 for World Service. As our target was $150.00, 
we were very pleased with this effort. Once again, we are indebted to 
Mr. and Mrs. Le Albert for the many items they donated to the Fair, and 
for their untiring efforts during the sale. 


CRAFTS: 

Woodwork in the Laddie Millen Craft Shop was the most popular 
of the crafts. Each camper had an opportunity to use the shop. Clay 
modelling, art, carving and archery were also popular. 


A few of the outstanding program events were Indian Day, Rodeos, 
Indian Decathlon, Swim Meets, Amateur Nights and Regattas. 


HEALTH AND SAFETY: 

The general health of the camp was very good. All 
ailments were of minor nature. Mrs. Sirkin was very thorough in her 
care. On arrival, each camper reported to the hospital and was inspect- 
ed from head to toe. 


-3- 


The average gain in weight was a little over two pounds per campere 
Dr. Kelso, camp doctor for many years, paid us several visits during 
the summer. We are deeply indebted to him for his help and friendly 
interest in the camp. 


MAINTENANCE 
BUILDINGS: All buildings are in good condition. The hump 


was taken out of the Craft Shop. The Parliaments, 
Wash House and all except two sides of the Hospital 
was painted this year. All galleries were given 
their annual coat of paint and the Dining Hall and 
Kitchen floors were varnished as usual. 


PARLIAMENTS : The Farliaments were emptied this year. 
‘THARVES: The Wharves are in good condition. 
REFRIGERATION: The Refrigeration worked satisfactory this summer. 
TENT PLATFCRMS: Many of the tent platforms were repaired but in 
general they are in poor condition. 
TENTS: Most of the tents are in good condition. 
RECOMMENDATIONS 


1. ‘hen renting a truck for Perrot, get one that looks respectable» 


2. Paint the dining hall and finish the hospital next spring. Paint 
the craft shop and cottage in the spring of 1960. 


3+ Repair the tent platforms and tent stairs as best we can without 
doing a major overhaul. 


4. Buy one or two new tents. 


Respectfully submitted, 


Donald Cochrane. 
Director,
